What the week actually proved

The entry discipline did the work, not the stock picking. Five of the six longs never triggered — and that was the right outcome, because every one of them fell. JNJ went from 275.23 to 265.58, BMY 66.82 to 63.64, TGT 164.44 to 155.83, NVDA 230.36 to 218.29. Had those been bought at the market on Monday instead of on a stop above the pivot, the long book would have lost roughly 3% across four names. Instead it lost nothing, because price never paid up and the orders never filled. That is the single most valuable property of a buy-stop-above-the-pivot rule and it is worth understanding before the next tempting-looking base.

Every short triggered and every short is green. All four filled within two sessions and none came close to a stop. NKE is the best at +0.44R. That is not skill — it is a risk-off week, and the short book was correctly positioned for one.

The wider screen says the same thing louder. Across all 42 names that passed either template, 14 broke their pivot (33%). Measured directionally — long candidates by their return, short candidates by the inverse — the 22 long candidates averaged -2.82% and the 20 short candidates +1.64%. The screen identified the right names on both sides; the tape only paid on one.

One week of ten trades proves nothing. A 100% win rate on five open positions is a sample, not an edge — and every one of those five is still open and can still give it all back. The honest read is narrower: the rules behaved as designed, the stop-entry filter saved money on the long side, and the defensive rotation called last week continued. Track this for a quarter before drawing any conclusion about whether the system makes money.

The logic, stated as rules

Every filter below is computed from split-adjusted daily OHLCV — nothing is discretionary, and nothing was chosen after seeing which names would pass. The rule set fuses four published frameworks: Weinstein's stage analysis for the regime a stock is in, Minervini's trend template for whether it is in a genuine Stage 2 advance, the Donchian / Turtle channel breakout for the trigger, and volatility contraction plus volume signature for whether the base is being accumulated or merely drifting.

Long — Stage 2 trend template (all seven must be true)

  1. Moving-average stack. Close > 50 SMA > 150 SMA > 200 SMA, and close above all three.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA higher than 21 sessions ago and 50 SMA higher than 10 sessions ago — the trend is being renewed, not decaying.
  3. Proximity to high. Within 25% of the 52-week high. Leadership does not hide in the bottom of its range.
  4. Distance from low. At least 25% above the 52-week low — filters out dead-cat bounces off a Stage 4 base.
  5. Relative strength. RS in the top 30% of the universe, where RS is the IBD-style weighted excess return over SPY: 40% × 3-month, 20% each × 6-, 9- and 12-month.
  6. Liquidity. 20-day average dollar volume ≥ $50M, so a 10–40 share-lot or a spread fills without slippage.
  7. Base structure. Range depth ≤ 18% measured over the shortest of the last 25, 40 or 60 sessions that qualifies.

Long — setup trigger (base rules plus these)

  • Proximity to pivot. Price within 7% of the base high — close enough that a buy stop is a trade, not a hope.
  • Not extended. No more than 14% above the 50 SMA. A stock already 3–5 ATR extended is a bad breakout buy regardless of how good the trend looks.
  • Volatility contraction or accumulation. Either ATR% today ≤ its level 20 sessions ago, or ATR% ≤ 0.85× its level 40 sessions ago (the VCP signature); or up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≥ 0.95.

Short — Stage 4 breakdown (all six must be true)

  1. Inverted stack. Close below both the 50 SMA and 200 SMA, and 50 SMA below 200 SMA.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA or 50 SMA declining — supply is in control on at least one timeframe.
  3. Proximity to low. No more than 25% above the 52-week low.
  4. Damage done. At least 18% below the 52-week high — this is a broken stock, not a pullback in an uptrend.
  5. Relative weakness. RS in the bottom 30% of the universe.
  6. Distribution. Up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≤ 1.05 — rallies are not being bought.

Trigger adds: price within 7% above the 25/40/60-session base low, and not more than 14% below the 50 SMA (an already-collapsed stock mean-reverts violently and is a poor short entry).

Entry, stop and target construction

  • Entry. Stop order at the structural pivot — the higher of the base high and the 20-day Donchian high for longs, the lower of the base low and the 20-day Donchian low for shorts — plus a 0.10 ATR buffer through the level. No anticipation, no limit orders inside the base.
  • Stop. The wider of the nearest structural level (10-day extreme, base extreme, or nearest clustered S/R zone) offset by 0.30 ATR, capped at 2.2 ATR from entry. The Turtle system's 2N stop, with structure allowed to tighten it but never to widen it past 2.2N.
  • Target 1. Entry ± 1.5R. Take a third to a half off; move the stop to breakeven.
  • Target 2. The measured move — base height projected from the pivot — or 2.8R, whichever is further.
  • Trail. After T1, trail on the 20-day Donchian extreme in the opposite direction (the Turtle System-2 exit).
  • Sizing. Shares = $500 ÷ (entry − stop), capped at 30% of account notional per position.

How the levels on each chart were derived

  • Swing highs / lows. Fractal pivots — a bar whose high is the strict maximum (or low the strict minimum) of the five bars either side of it. Marked ▼ and ▲ on the charts.
  • Support / resistance zones. Three-bar fractal pivots from the last 15 months, clustered where they fall within 0.6 ATR of each other. Each zone carries a touch count and the date it was last tested — a level touched four times is a different object from one touched once.
  • Volume profile. Six months of daily bars, 80 price bins, each bar's volume distributed uniformly across its high–low range. POC is the highest-volume bin; the value area is the 70% of volume around it; HVN are local maxima above the 75th percentile (shaded purple — price tends to stall and rotate there); LVN are local minima below the 25th percentile (grey dotted — price tends to move through them quickly).
  • Donchian channels. 20-day and 55-day extremes, excluding the current bar.

Sources

Minervini trend template criteria — Deepvue, TraderLion on stage analysis. Donchian breakout lengths, the N/ATR volatility unit, 2N stop and 20-day trailing exit — the original Turtle trading rules. Volume-profile HVN/LVN/POC methodology — AlgoVistra, FXOpen on fixed-range volume profile. Price data via Yahoo Finance; live quotes, option chains, Greeks and the earnings calendar via the connected brokerage MCP.

Market regime

Everything got worse underneath. The indices still sit above rising 50- and 200-day averages, but every internal measure deteriorated over the week: breadth fell, Stage 2 thinned, Stage 4 widened, and the VIX turned up 11% off a complacent base. Stage 4 names now outnumber Stage 2 names for the first time since this report began — 12.4% against 11.2%. That crossover is the headline.

Last week's report set a stand-down rule and the tape has now hit it. The rule read: "if the percentage of the universe above its 50 SMA falls under 45%, breakouts fail at a much higher rate; trade the shorts and stand down on the longs." Breadth closed Friday at exactly 45.0%, down from 49.1%. That is the threshold, not past it — so this is not an instruction to abandon the long book, but it is the point at which long-side size should be cut rather than added to. The long candidate count fell from 18 setup-ready to 11; the short count rose from 13 to 16. The screen is voting the same way.

What the leadership is telling you

The defensive rotation called last week not only continued, it concentrated. Energy is now the clear long-side leader — COP, CVX, XOM and FANG all pass, and COP is the only name in the entire screen whose score improved week over week. Financials hold second place through MET, JPM and BAC. The short side is still consumer discretionary and staples retail, now joined by health-care equipment: IDXX, GEHC and ABT are new stage-4 entrants, which is a fresh group breaking down rather than more of the same.

Two names changed the tech story. NVDA dropped out of the long screen entirely after falling 5.2% on the week — last week's only megacap tech long is gone. AAPL replaced it, and did so the right way: it rose while QQQ fell. One name is not a sector, but it is the only evidence in this report that megacap technology is not uniformly distributing.

The correlation warning from last week stands and has tightened. Four of the ten plans below are positions you already hold. The long book is energy and financials; the short book is consumer and health-care equipment. Both sides are the same rotation trade expressed twice — they win together and they lose together.

Why some high scorers were not given plans

Three filters were applied on top of the raw ranking. Sector concentration — health care produced seven of the 22 long passers (JNJ, BMY, BIIB, VRTX, AMGN, DXCM, MRK); taking the top two rather than the top four keeps a single FDA or drug-pricing headline from hitting four positions at once, which is why BIIB (77.5) and VRTX (76.1) were dropped despite outranking NVDA. The same logic removed HD on the short side, since LOW already carries the home-improvement trade. Setup-ready only — MRK, ILMN, ABNB and CRWD pass the trend template but fail a trigger condition, mostly base depth above 18%. Extension — LULU (91.2) and APP (75.5) score well as shorts but sit 15% and 18.6% below their 50-day averages; entering there invites a mean-reversion squeeze.

Read this before placing anything

Four of the ten are positions you already have on. CVX, MCD, NKE and PEP triggered last week and are still open, carrying $1,733.54 of live risk between them. Their cards below show an entry price, but for those four that line is an add level, not a new trade. Treating it as new doubles the position and doubles the risk. What actually changed for them is the stop and the targets, which have been rolled forward with the new data — those supersede last week's numbers.

That leaves 6 genuinely new setups — COP, MET, JPM, AAPL, BIIB and IDXX — worth $2,961.19 if every one triggers, which they will not.

  • Cut the live cap to 3–4 positions. Breadth at 45.0% is the stand-down threshold this report set last week. Fewer new longs, not more.
  • Do not re-enter the four you already own. Manage them on the revised stops.
  • Favour the short side and energy. Those are the only two groups the tape actually paid last week (shorts +1.64% directionally, energy the sole improving long group).
  • Let the trigger choose. Five of six longs did not fill last week and that saved real money. Place the stop orders and let price decide — do not anticipate.
  • Below 40% breadth, stop taking new longs entirely and run the short book alone.

Execution notes

  • Monday 2026-09-14 is the next session — a normal week, no holiday. If a stock gaps through its trigger by more than 0.5 ATR, stand aside rather than chasing; the risk:reward the plan was built on no longer exists.
  • Two names have no usable option market. BIIB and IDXX Oct-16 chains are not tradeable — zero bids, single-digit open interest, spreads wider than the edge. Their cards say so instead of printing a mid-price you could not fill. Shares only.
  • AAPL cannot be sized inside the risk budget as a spread. One contract loses about $662 at the stop and one contract is the minimum. Use the 28 shares.
  • Confirm the breakout on volume. A trigger that fires on below-average volume is a lower-quality signal. The plan does not enforce this mechanically, but a breakout day below 1.2× the 50-day average volume deserves a half-size entry.
  • Options are for the trend, not the trigger. All ten structures are 38-DTE debit verticals expiring 2026-10-16. If a trade stops out in the first week, you lose roughly the delta-adjusted amount shown in each card, not the full debit — that is the basis contract counts were sized on. If you cannot honour the stop, trade shares instead.
  • Three names report before the Oct-16 expiry: NKE on 2026-10-01, PEP on 2026-10-08, JPM on 2026-10-13 — all confirmed. Close or roll each before its print. PEP is new to this list.
  • Re-run the scan on any 2%+ index day. Base depths, Donchian levels and the pivot itself move; a plan built on Friday's close is stale after a large directional session.

What would invalidate this whole report

Unchanged from last week, and now closer on one side. A VIX move above roughly 22 with SPY losing its 50-day average (758.62, only 0.7% below Friday's close) puts the market in a regime where long breakouts fail systematically and the short book should be the only book. The opposite case — a breadth thrust back through 65% above the 50 SMA — would mean the defensive rotation is finished, the short candidates are about to squeeze hard, and the leadership list needs rebuilding from scratch. Breadth is at 45% and falling, so the first case is the live risk and the second is the one that would hurt the current book most.
